summary:
Algeria criminalises same-sex sexual activity under the Penal Code of 1966, Ordinance 66-156 of 8 June 1966. Article 338 punishes a homosexual act with 2 months to 2 years imprisonment and a fine of 500 to 2,000 Algerian dinars and applies to both male and female same-sex conduct. The United States Department of State 2023 human rights report describes the offence as undefined homosexual acts carrying 2 months to 2 years imprisonment plus fines. The United Kingdom Home Office country policy note of 26 July 2026 confirms the 1966 Code remains the operative framework, citing a Human Dignity Trust legal summary updated in June 2026.

Article 338 provides an aggravated penalty where one participant is below 18 years of age, with up to 3 years imprisonment and a 10,000 dinars fine for the older participant. Article 333 separately punishes outrage to public decency consisting of an act against nature with a person of the same sex with 6 months to 3 years imprisonment and a fine of 1,000 to 10,000 Algerian dinars.

Enforcement is documented. Non-governmental organisations report arrests within the LGBT+ community, with little information on the trans identity of those arrested. On 24 July 2020 police raided a private home in el-Kharoub, Constantine Province, and arrested 44 people, 9 women and 35 men, mostly university students, over an alleged gay wedding. On 3 September 2020 a court sentenced 2 to imprisonment and 42 to suspended terms, relying on decorations and gay appearance as evidence.

Algeria provides no statutory route for gender transition. Civil-status gender-marker changes are theoretically blocked, with no legal gender-recognition procedure available.

Algeria has no legal framework for gender-affirming healthcare. Medical and surgical gender-affirming care is prohibited. Articles 274 and 264 of the penal framework could be used against providers, producing de facto criminalisation of provision.

Detained LGBTQI+ persons have no specific legal protections. Prison authorities separate persons deemed vulnerable, but no distinct protection applies to LGBTQI+ detainees. Civil society organisations report compounded discrimination against LGBTQI+ persons. The law does not recognise or respect the civil rights of LGBTQ persons.

Same-sex partnership has no recognition. Most attempts at unofficial same-sex marriage are blocked by police, including a documented attempt in 2005.
tangentialFactors:
The criminal provisions originate in prevailing mores that view homosexuality and cross-dressing as contrary to the Islamic faith.

Homophobic attitudes are normalised. The prevailing social attitude toward homosexuality is described as openly negative and at times violent. LGBTQ persons are commonly subjected to discrimination and potential arrest. A 2018-19 Arab Barometer survey found about 26 percent of Algerians considered homosexuality should be accepted.

Vigilante executions, beatings and torture have occurred, with police frequently joining the attacks, participating as accomplices, or turning a blind eye. Documented cases include the stoning of two men in the street in 2001 and the killing of two men in 1994 and 1996 described as hate crimes against homosexuals.

In 2019 Assil Belatla, a student suspected of being gay, was murdered in his university-district dormitory, with the words he is gay painted on the wall with his blood, in circumstances where the killer believed he would avoid prosecution. Following the 2019 death of Houari Manar, a popular rai singer widely thought to be gay, homophobic comments were posted on social media.
localsOnly:
United Kingdom asylum guidance assesses internal relocation as viable for gay men, while lesbians and trans women face societal difficulties on relocation. Refusals in such cases are rarely certified as clearly unfounded.

No political organisation is permitted to campaign for LGBTQ rights in Algeria. Officially there are no gay-friendly establishments.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved as to transgender-specific criminal liability: no transgender-specific offence, penalty, imprisonment term, fine, age threshold, enforcement action, arrest or case outcome for cross-dressing or transgender identity itself is sourced.

Not sourced as to transgender-specific administrative rules: no document rule, screening procedure, facility rule, custody rule, care rule beyond the general prohibition, or protection mechanism specific to transgender persons is documented.

Unresolved as to enforcement breakdown: arrests of LGBT+ persons are reported without information on how many of those arrested were trans, so a trans-specific enforcement rate cannot be stated.

Not sourced as to societal tolerance of transgender persons specifically: available tolerance and attitude statements concern homosexuality and homophobia, with no documented statement on attitudes toward transgender persons alone.
